en-B1-0.b:
The present perfect continuous = have/has been + verb-ing. It describes an activity that started in the past and is still continuing or has just stopped with visible results.

  • Duration with for / since: I've been learning Dutch for six months. She's been working here since 2021.
  • Recent activity with results: Why are you wet? — I've been running.
  • Question: How long have you been waiting?

for + period (for two hours); since + starting point (since Monday, since 9 o'clock).

Compare: I've been reading this book (activity, not finished) / I've read this book (finished, result).

State verbs stay simple: I've known him for years (not « been knowing »).

Common mistake (French influence): « I live here since 2020 » → I've been living / I've lived here since 2020.
en-B1-0.t:
Le present perfect continuous = have/has been + verbe-ing. Il décrit une activité commencée dans le passé qui continue encore ou qui vient de s'arrêter avec des résultats visibles.

  • Durée avec for / since : I've been learning Dutch for six months. (J'apprends le néerlandais depuis six mois) She's been working here since 2021.
  • Activité récente avec résultat : Why are you wet? — I've been running.
  • Question : How long have you been waiting? (Depuis combien de temps attends-tu ?)

for + durée (for two hours) ; since + point de départ (since Monday, since 9 o'clock).

Compare : I've been reading this book (activité, pas finie) / I've read this book (fini, résultat).

Les verbes d'état restent simples : I've known him for years (pas « been knowing »).

Erreur fréquente (influence du français « depuis » + présent) : « I live here since 2020 » → I've been living / I've lived here since 2020.
e: I've been learning Dutch for six months.
How long have you been waiting?
She's been working here since 2021.
It's been raining all day.
I'm tired because I've been studying.
q: I ___ Dutch for a year. (learn, still)

en-B1-1.b:
The past perfect = had + past participle. It shows that one past action happened before another past action.

  • When I arrived, the film had already started.
  • She told me she had lost her keys.
  • I had never seen snow before I moved to Belgium.

Same form for all persons: I/you/he/they had gone. Contraction: I'd gone.

Time words: already, just, never… before, by the time, after, when.

If the order is clear (with before / after), the past simple is also possible: I left after I (had) finished.

Past perfect continuous: I had been waiting for an hour when he arrived.

Common mistake: using the past simple for both actions when the order matters: When I got to the station, the train had left (not « left », which means it left as I arrived).
en-B1-1.t:
Le past perfect = had + participe passé. Il montre qu'une action passée s'est produite avant une autre action passée (= plus-que-parfait).

  • When I arrived, the film had already started.
  • She told me she had lost her keys.
  • I had never seen snow before I moved to Belgium.

Même forme à toutes les personnes : I/you/he/they had gone. Contraction : I'd gone.

Mots de temps : already, just, never… before, by the time (au moment où), after, when.

Si l'ordre est clair (avec before / after), le prétérit est aussi possible : I left after I (had) finished.

Past perfect continu : I had been waiting for an hour when he arrived.

Erreur fréquente : utiliser le prétérit pour les deux actions quand l'ordre compte : When I got to the station, the train had left (pas « left », qui voudrait dire qu'il partait au moment où j'arrivais).
e: When we arrived, everyone had already left.
I had never flown before that trip.
She said she had finished the report.
By the time he called, I had gone to bed.
They had been living in Paris for years before they moved.
q: I ___ never seen the sea before.
By the time we got there, the shop ___ (close)
He ___ been waiting for an hour.
After she ___ dinner, she went out.

en-B1-2.b:
used to + verb describes past habits or states that are no longer true.

  • I used to live in Congo. (I don't anymore)
  • She used to smoke, but she stopped.
  • Negative/question: I didn't use to like vegetables. Did you use to play football?

would + verb also describes repeated past actions (often in stories), but not states: Every summer, we would go to the coast. (but not « I would live in Congo »).

Don't confuse:

  • used to do = past habit
  • be used to doing = be accustomed to: I'm used to getting up early.
  • get used to doing = become accustomed: I'm getting used to the Belgian weather.

Common mistake: « I use to live » (present) → I used to live; « I'm used to get up » → I'm used to getting up.
en-B1-2.t:
used to + verbe décrit des habitudes ou états passés qui ne sont plus vrais (= l'imparfait d'habitude).

  • I used to live in Congo. (J'habitais au Congo — plus maintenant)
  • She used to smoke, but she stopped.
  • Négation/question : I didn't use to like vegetables. Did you use to play football?

would + verbe décrit aussi des actions répétées au passé (souvent dans un récit), mais pas des états : Every summer, we would go to the coast. (mais pas « I would live in Congo »).

Ne pas confondre :

  • used to do = habitude passée
  • be used to doing = être habitué à : I'm used to getting up early.
  • get used to doing = s'habituer à : I'm getting used to the Belgian weather.

Erreur fréquente : « I use to live » (au présent) → I used to live ; « I'm used to get up » → I'm used to getting up.
e: I used to play football every weekend.
She didn't use to like coffee.
When I was a kid, my grandmother would tell us stories.
I'm used to working at night.
You'll get used to the rain.
q: Past state (not would): I ___ have long hair.
Every Sunday, we ___ visit my grandparents. (story)
"Je suis habitué au froid" = I'm used to ___

en-B1-3.b:
The second conditional talks about imaginary, unlikely or impossible situations in the present or future.

If + past simple, would + verb:

  • If I had more money, I would travel the world.
  • If I lived in Antwerp, I would speak Dutch every day.
  • What would you do if you won the lottery?

With be, formal English uses were for all persons: If I were you, I would accept. (advice)

could / might are possible instead of would: If I had time, I could help you.

Compare: If it rains, I'll stay home (1st: possible) / If it snowed in July, I'd be surprised (2nd: unlikely).

Common mistake: « If I would have money » → If I had money (no would after if).
en-B1-3.t:
Le deuxième conditionnel parle de situations imaginaires, peu probables ou impossibles au présent ou au futur.

If + prétérit, would + verbe (= si + imparfait, conditionnel) :

  • If I had more money, I would travel the world.
  • If I lived in Antwerp, I would speak Dutch every day.
  • What would you do if you won the lottery?

Avec be, l'anglais soutenu utilise were à toutes les personnes : If I were you, I would accept. (À ta place, j'accepterais)

could / might peuvent remplacer would : If I had time, I could help you.

Compare : If it rains, I'll stay home (1er : possible) / If it snowed in July, I'd be surprised (2e : peu probable).

Erreur fréquente : « If I would have money » → If I had money (pas de would après if).
e: If I had a car, I would drive to work.
If I were you, I'd learn Dutch.
What would you do if you lost your job?
If she spoke Dutch, she could work in Ghent.
I wouldn't do that if I were you.
q: If I ___ rich, I would buy a house.
If I had time, I ___ help you.
What would you do if you ___ the lottery? (win)
If I ___ in Ghent, I would speak Dutch. (live)
If I would have time, I would come.
If I had time, I would come.
If I had time, I will come.
I ___ do that if I were you. (negative)

en-B1-4.b:
The passive focuses on the action or the person/thing affected, not on who does it.

be + past participle:

  • Present simple: English is spoken here.
  • Past simple: The bridge was built in 1900.
  • Present continuous: The road is being repaired.
  • Present perfect: My bike has been stolen.
  • With modals: It must be done today.

The agent with by (only if important): The film was directed by a Belgian.

Use it when the doer is unknown, obvious or unimportant: My car was stolen. (by whom? unknown)

English uses the passive more than French: « On m'a dit que… » → I was told that…

Common mistake: forgetting be: « The house built in 1900 » → The house was built…
en-B1-4.t:
Le passif met l'accent sur l'action ou sur la personne/chose concernée, pas sur celui qui agit.

be + participe passé :

  • Présent simple : English is spoken here. (On parle anglais ici)
  • Prétérit : The bridge was built in 1900.
  • Présent continu : The road is being repaired. (La route est en réparation)
  • Present perfect : My bike has been stolen.
  • Avec un modal : It must be done today.

L'agent avec by (seulement s'il est important) : The film was directed by a Belgian.

On l'utilise quand l'auteur est inconnu, évident ou sans importance : My car was stolen.

L'anglais utilise le passif plus que le français : « On m'a dit que… » → I was told that…

Erreur fréquente : oublier be : « The house built in 1900 » → The house was built…
e: Dutch is spoken in Flanders.
The museum was opened in 1885.
My wallet has been stolen.
The new station is being built.
I was told the meeting was cancelled.
q: The book was written ___ a Belgian author.

en-B1-5.b:
Reported speech tells what someone said. When the reporting verb is in the past (said, told), the tense usually moves one step back:

DirectReported
present simple: "I am tired"past simple: she said she was tired
present continuous: "I'm working"past continuous: he said he was working
past simple / present perfectpast perfect: he said he had seen it
willwould
cancould
  • say (no person): She said (that)… · tell + person: She told me (that)…
  • Questions: normal word order + if/whether or question word: He asked if I was ready. She asked where I lived.
  • Orders: tell/ask + person + to: He told me to wait.
  • Time words: today → that day, tomorrow → the next day, yesterday → the day before.

Common mistake: « She said me » → She told me / She said to me; « He asked where did I live » → where I lived.
en-B1-5.t:
Le discours indirect rapporte ce que quelqu'un a dit. Quand le verbe introducteur est au passé (said, told), le temps recule d'un cran :

DirectIndirect
présent simple : "I am tired"prétérit : she said she was tired
présent continu : "I'm working"past continuous : he said he was working
prétérit / present perfectpast perfect : he said he had seen it
willwould
cancould
  • say (sans personne) : She said (that)… · tell + personne : She told me (that)…
  • Questions : ordre normal + if/whether ou mot interrogatif : He asked if I was ready. She asked where I lived.
  • Ordres : tell/ask + personne + to : He told me to wait.
  • Mots de temps : today → that day, tomorrow → the next day, yesterday → the day before.

Erreur fréquente : « She said me » → She told me / She said to me ; « He asked where did I live » → where I lived.
e: She said she was tired.
He told me he would call later.
They asked if I spoke Dutch.
My boss told me to finish the report.
She asked where the station was.
q: "I am tired." → She said she ___ tired.
"I will call." → He said he ___ call.
"I saw it." → He said he ___ it.

en-B1-6.b:
Relative clauses give more information about a noun.

  • who: people: The woman who lives next door is a nurse.
  • which: things, animals: The car which I bought is red.
  • that: people or things (informal, defining clauses): The film that we saw was great.
  • where: places: the town where I was born
  • whose: possession: the man whose car was stolen

You can omit who/which/that when it is the object: The book (that) I'm reading is good. But not when it's the subject: The man who called…

Non-defining clauses (extra info) use commas and never that: My brother, who lives in Liège, is a doctor.

Common mistake: « The man which… » → The man who…; « My car, that is new, … » → My car, which is new, …
en-B1-6.t:
Les propositions relatives donnent plus d'informations sur un nom.

  • who : personnes : The woman who lives next door is a nurse.
  • which : choses, animaux : The car which I bought is red.
  • that : personnes ou choses (familier, relatives déterminatives) : The film that we saw was great.
  • where : lieux (où) : the town where I was born
  • whose : possession (dont) : the man whose car was stolen

On peut omettre who/which/that quand c'est le complément : The book (that) I'm reading is good. Mais pas quand c'est le sujet : The man who called…

Les relatives explicatives (info en plus) ont des virgules et jamais that : My brother, who lives in Liège, is a doctor.

Erreur fréquente : « The man which… » → The man who… ; « My car, that is new, … » → My car, which is new, …
e: The colleague who helped me is from Ghent.
This is the house where I grew up.
The book I'm reading is fascinating.
My sister, who lives in Brussels, is a lawyer.
That's the man whose dog bit me.
q: The man ___ called you is my boss.
The car ___ I bought is blue.
the woman ___ son is a doctor
Can be omitted: The book ___ I read was good.
My brother, ___ lives in Liège, is 30.
My phone, ___ is new, doesn't work.
The people ___ work here are friendly.

en-B1-7.b:
Modals of deduction show how sure you are about something.

certaintypresentpast
almost sure: yesmust bemust have been
possiblemight / may / could bemight / may / could have been
almost sure: nocan't becan't / couldn't have been
  • She's not answering. She must be busy.
  • Take an umbrella; it might rain.
  • That can't be true! (opposite of must is can't, not « mustn't »)
  • Past: The streets are wet. It must have rained. He might have missed the bus.

Common mistake: « It mustn't be true » (deduction) → It can't be true; « He must went » → He must have gone.
en-B1-7.t:
Les modaux de déduction montrent ton degré de certitude.

certitudeprésentpassé
presque sûr : ouimust be (doit être)must have been (a dû être)
possiblemight / may / could bemight / may / could have been
presque sûr : noncan't be (ne peut pas être)can't / couldn't have been
  • She's not answering. She must be busy. (Elle doit être occupée)
  • Take an umbrella; it might rain. (il se peut qu'il pleuve)
  • That can't be true! (le contraire de must est can't, pas « mustn't »)
  • Passé : The streets are wet. It must have rained. He might have missed the bus.

Erreur fréquente : « It mustn't be true » (déduction) → It can't be true ; « He must went » → He must have gone.
e: You must be tired after that trip.
She might be at home, I'm not sure.
That can't be right.
He must have forgotten our meeting.
They may have missed the train.
q: He's not answering. He ___ be asleep. (almost sure)
The ground is wet. It ___ rained.
She ___ have seen us; she didn't say hello. (possible)
He ___ have done it; he was with me. (impossible)
Correct past: He must ___ the bus.

en-B1-8.b:
Phrasal verbs = verb + particle (up, out, off, on, down, back…). The meaning is often different from the verb alone. Natives use them all the time.

  • get up (se lever) · wake up · turn on/off (allumer/éteindre) · put on (mettre un vêtement) · take off (enlever / décoller)
  • look for (chercher) · look after (s'occuper de) · find out (découvrir) · give up (abandonner) · carry on (continuer)
  • pick up (ramasser / aller chercher) · fill in (remplir un formulaire) · run out of (manquer de) · come back · go out (sortir)

Separable verbs: the object can go in the middle; a pronoun must: Turn the light off / Turn off the light / Turn it off (not « turn off it »).

Inseparable: look for it, look after them.

Common mistake: « Turn off it » → Turn it off; translating literally instead of using the phrasal verb (continue → carry on in speech).
en-B1-8.t:
Les verbes à particule (phrasal verbs) = verbe + particule (up, out, off, on, down, back…). Le sens est souvent différent du verbe seul. Les natifs les utilisent tout le temps.

  • get up (se lever) · wake up (se réveiller) · turn on/off (allumer/éteindre) · put on (mettre un vêtement) · take off (enlever / décoller)
  • look for (chercher) · look after (s'occuper de) · find out (découvrir) · give up (abandonner) · carry on (continuer)
  • pick up (ramasser / aller chercher) · fill in (remplir un formulaire) · run out of (manquer de) · come back (revenir) · go out (sortir)

Verbes séparables : le complément peut aller au milieu ; un pronom doit y aller : Turn the light off / Turn off the light / Turn it off (pas « turn off it »).

Inséparables : look for it, look after them.

Erreur fréquente : « Turn off it » → Turn it off ; traduire mot à mot au lieu d'utiliser le phrasal verb (continue → carry on à l'oral).
e: I get up at seven every day.
Can you turn the music down?
I'm looking for my keys.
Don't give up, you're almost there!
We've run out of milk.
q: I'll ___ you ___ at the station. (aller chercher)

en-B1-9.b:
Question tags are short questions at the end of a sentence, to check information or invite agreement (= n'est-ce pas ?).

  • Positive sentence → negative tag: You're Belgian, aren't you?
  • Negative sentence → positive tag: She doesn't smoke, does she?
  • Use the same auxiliary (be, do, have, can, will…): He can swim, can't he? They went home, didn't they? You've finished, haven't you?
  • Pronoun, not noun: Tom is nice, isn't he?

Special cases: I'm late, aren't I? Let's go, shall we? Open the door, will you? · Negative words (never, nobody) → positive tag: He never calls, does he?

Intonation: falling = I expect agreement; rising = real question.

Common mistake: using « isn't it? » for everything → choose the right auxiliary.
en-B1-9.t:
Les question tags sont de petites questions en fin de phrase pour vérifier une info ou chercher l'accord (= n'est-ce pas ?).

  • Phrase affirmative → tag négatif : You're Belgian, aren't you?
  • Phrase négative → tag affirmatif : She doesn't smoke, does she?
  • Même auxiliaire (be, do, have, can, will…) : He can swim, can't he? They went home, didn't they? You've finished, haven't you?
  • Un pronom, pas un nom : Tom is nice, isn't he?

Cas particuliers : I'm late, aren't I? Let's go, shall we? Open the door, will you? · Mots négatifs (never, nobody) → tag affirmatif : He never calls, does he?

Intonation : descendante = j'attends l'accord ; montante = vraie question.

Erreur fréquente : utiliser « isn't it? » partout → choisis le bon auxiliaire.
e: It's cold today, isn't it?
You speak French, don't you?
She hasn't called yet, has she?
They'll come, won't they?
Let's take a break, shall we?

en-B1-10.b:
The future continuous = will be + verb-ing. It describes an action that will be in progress at a specific time in the future.

  • This time tomorrow, I'll be flying to Brussels.
  • At 8 pm, we'll be having dinner.
  • Don't call at 10; I'll be sleeping.

It is also used for polite questions about plans (you don't want to pressure the person): Will you be using the car tonight?

And for things that will happen as part of a normal routine: I'll be seeing Tom at work anyway.

Negative: I won't be working on Friday.

Common mistake: « This time tomorrow I will fly » (in progress) → I'll be flying.
en-B1-10.t:
Le futur continu = will be + verbe-ing. Il décrit une action qui sera en cours à un moment précis du futur.

  • This time tomorrow, I'll be flying to Brussels. (Demain à cette heure-ci, je serai en vol)
  • At 8 pm, we'll be having dinner.
  • Don't call at 10; I'll be sleeping.

Il sert aussi pour des questions polies sur les projets (sans mettre de pression) : Will you be using the car tonight?

Et pour ce qui arrivera dans le cours normal des choses : I'll be seeing Tom at work anyway.

Négation : I won't be working on Friday.

Erreur fréquente : « This time tomorrow I will fly » (action en cours) → I'll be flying.
e: This time next week, I'll be lying on a beach.
Don't call me at nine, I'll be driving.
Will you be needing anything else?
I won't be working on Monday.
At 6 pm, we'll be having dinner.
q: This time tomorrow I ___ to Ghent. (travel)
Polite: ___ you be using the car tonight?
In ten years, she ___ living abroad.
___ you be coming to the party?
